name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,316

entries.clue: Follow some milk carts heading west (5)

indicatorNotes.some: only part of the phrase is used, so the letters sit inside it
indicatorNotes.heading west: an across entry reads west to east, so heading west means read right to left

blocks.note: the letters run consecutively across the word break in milK CARTs

annotation.surface: A milk float trundling off towards the west at dawn.
annotation.walkthrough: The span straddles two words, and the carts' westward trip is really an order to read the letters right to left.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the verb sense: you trail a quarry by its tracks, the marks it leaves behind.

entries.clue: Article on Financial Times robbery (5)

annotation.surface: A newspaper feature reporting on a robbery.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads like a news story about a heist; in fact 'Article' is the grammar kind, and the paper is only its initials. In a down entry the article simply sits on top.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: strictly a robbery uses force and a theft need not, but everyday usage treats them as the same crime of stealing.

entries.clue: Struggled in San Diego after surgery (8)

indicatorNotes.after surgery: something operated on has had its parts rearranged

annotation.surface: A patient having a rough recovery in a California hospital.
annotation.walkthrough: The city is not a place here but eight letters to rearrange. AGONISED is the British spelling; AGONIZED would not fit the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: To agonise over something is to struggle with it.

entries.clue: Cricketer, one you don’t want to lose? (6)

annotation.definition2: one you don’t want to lose

blocks.note: the fielder who stands behind the stumps

blocks.clueFragment: one you don’t want to lose
blocks.note: informal praise for a partner or possession worth holding onto

annotation.surface: A captain reluctant to drop a valued player.
annotation.walkthrough: In cricket the wicket-keeper, usually just the keeper, crouches behind the stumps to catch the ball; the question mark flags the second, informal sense.
annotation.definitionFit: The wicket-keeper is a cricketer, and something worth keeping is a keeper.

entries.clue: Field marshal married in capital at end of April (6)

indicatorNotes.in: M is put inside the capital
indicatorNotes.at end of: takes the final letter of April and places it last

blocks.note: the Italian capital, split to take a letter

annotation.surface: A military man getting married in a capital city in spring.
annotation.walkthrough: The spring wedding is a false scene; 'end of April' is a single letter, not a date. Erwin Rommel was the German 'Desert Fox'.
annotation.definitionFit: Rommel held the rank of field marshal in the German army.

entries.clue: Cautions against keeping account of heroic deeds (4)

indicatorNotes.keeping: the first words hold the answer inside them

blocks.note: the letters run consecutively across the word break in cautionS AGAinst

annotation.surface: Warnings not to keep a record of daring exploits.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cautions against' reads as a verb phrase, but it is only a string of letters hiding a four-letter word.
annotation.definitionFit: A saga is a long story of heroic deeds, originally Norse.

entries.clue: Very happy after bishop delayed (7)

indicatorNotes.after: sends 'Very happy' after the bishop, so B comes first

blocks.note: B = bishop, as in chess notation

annotation.surface: A cheerful cleric running late.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue reads as someone pleased once the bishop has been, but 'after' is instructing where to put the pieces.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: belated greetings or thanks arrive after their proper time, held up.

entries.clue: One page is fabricated — work of the CIA? (9)

indicatorNotes.fabricated: made up, so the letters are put together in a new way

annotation.surface: A forged dossier page, the sort of thing an intelligence agency might plant.
annotation.walkthrough: The forged document fits the spy theme so neatly that 'fabricated' reads as plain description rather than an instruction to rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: The CIA is the US intelligence agency, and spying is its work.

entries.clue: Noisy presence troubled priest let go (11)

indicatorNotes.troubled: disturbed, so the letters are stirred up

annotation.surface: An exorcist priest who was dismissed after a haunting went badly.
annotation.walkthrough: The priest belongs in a ghost story, which is what makes this one satisfying: the fodder and the answer share a scene.
annotation.definitionFit: A poltergeist is a ghost known for banging and throwing things.

entries.clue: Call up the day before to secure permission (5)

indicatorNotes.to secure: the eve holds the permission inside it

blocks.note: the eve is the day before an event
to give the OK is to give permission

annotation.surface: Phoning the day before to get the go-ahead.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Call up' looks like a phone call; here it means summon to mind.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, from Latin evocare, literally to call out, as a smell brings back a childhood summer.

entries.clue: American entertained by Greek character’s sexy dance (7)

indicatorNotes.entertained by: a guest is taken in by the host, so A goes inside

blocks.note: the Greek letter L, split to take the guest

annotation.surface: An American visitor enjoying a Greek host's provocative dance.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Greek character' suggests a person, but it is a letter of the Greek alphabet.
annotation.definitionFit: The lambada is a Brazilian dance famous for its close, sensual moves.

entries.clue: Weapon I initially dumped in river (7)

indicatorNotes.initially: takes only the first letter of 'dumped'
indicatorNotes.in: puts I and D inside the river

blocks.note: the Trent, a major river in the English Midlands, split to take two letters

annotation.surface: Someone getting rid of a weapon by throwing it in a river.
annotation.walkthrough: It is tempting to read 'I initially' as the letter I on its own; 'initially' actually acts on 'dumped'. The Trent is one of England's longest rivers.
annotation.definitionFit: A trident is a three-pronged spear, a weapon.

entries.clue: Cover up cuts in case of escape (7)

indicatorNotes.in: the cuts end up in the outer letters, so they are placed inside that shell
indicatorNotes.case of: the outside letters of a word, like its casing

annotation.surface: A cover-up involving budget cuts in a prison-break case.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Case' suggests an investigation, but it means the outer shell of the word 'escape'.
annotation.definitionFit: To eclipse something is to block it from view, to cover it up.

entries.clue: Keep substitute under pressure (8)

indicatorNotes.under: in a down entry, the substitute sits below pressure, so P comes first

blocks.note: a reserve player is a substitute

annotation.surface: Holding on to a replacement player when things get tense.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Under pressure' reads as a phrase about stress, but 'under' is placing a piece in the column.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of saving from harm or decay, as fruit is kept in jars.

entries.clue: Mostly impressive poem about singular experience (7)

indicatorNotes.Mostly: most of a word but not all of it, so the final letter of the adjective is dropped
indicatorNotes.about: loose: the poem is about the singular, so S sits alongside it, just before

annotation.surface: An ambitious poem written about one unique event.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About' usually means one piece goes round another; here it only sets S beside the poem, a loose instruction the setter relies on the other pieces to settle.
annotation.definitionFit: An episode is a single event or experience in someone's life.

entries.clue: Quietly totting up unnecessary words (7)

annotation.definitionNote: PADDING is a mass noun, while the definition is a plural phrase; padding is material made of unnecessary words.

blocks.note: to tot up is to add

annotation.surface: Someone quietly counting how many words in a text are surplus.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Quietly' looks like an adverb for the counting, but it supplies the musical P.
annotation.definitionFit: Padding is filler: words added to stretch a text without adding sense.

entries.clue: Republic is against return of old king (6)

indicatorNotes.against: placed next to, so the king follows IS
indicatorNotes.return of: a return is a journey back, so the king's name is read backwards, which in a down entry means bottom to top

blocks.note: LEAR, the ancient British king of Shakespeare's play, turned round

annotation.surface: A republic opposing the restoration of an old monarch.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is political, but 'return of old king' means the king's name turned round, not a restoration.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the state is one of many countries governed with an elected head rather than a monarch.

entries.clue: Ship carrying fruit for Britney? (6)

indicatorNotes.carrying: the ship holds the fruit inside it

annotation.surface: A cargo ship delivering fruit to a pop star.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is by example: Britney is a first name, and the question mark says the answer is her surname, as in the singer Britney Spears.
annotation.definitionFit: Britney Spears is the pop singer, so SPEARS completes 'Britney'.

entries.clue: Old flame sat out in the open (7)

blocks.note: sat for a portrait or photograph

annotation.surface: A former lover sitting outdoors.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sat out' looks like a phrase, but 'sat' ends the wordplay and 'out' begins the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: left without shelter or cover, whether a hillside or a secret.

entries.clue: Ready for marriage? (5)

blocks.note: the surface reading: prepared to wed
the intended reading: ready money, cash, as in 'the readies', paid for a marriage

annotation.surface: Someone asking whether a couple is prepared to wed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ready' is an adjective in the surface, but read it as the noun, ready cash. 'The readies' is British slang for money.
annotation.definitionFit: A dowry is money or property a bride's family pays on marriage.

entries.clue: Clumsily I arm a US soldier (7)

indicatorNotes.Clumsily: done badly, so the letters come out jumbled

annotation.surface: Someone awkwardly issuing a weapon to an American soldier.
annotation.walkthrough: 'US soldier' reads as one unit, a GI, but 'US' is fodder and 'soldier' alone is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: these were the hereditary military class of feudal Japan.

entries.clue: Reportedly failed to notice fog (4)

indicatorNotes.Reportedly: as it is said, pointing to a sound-alike

blocks.note: failed to notice = missed, which is pronounced like the answer

annotation.surface: A report of someone who overlooked the fog.
annotation.walkthrough: The past tense and the weather word are said identically.
annotation.definitionFit: A near synonym: both are water droplets hanging in the air, and meteorologists only split them by how far you can see.

entries.clue: An argument about right indicator? (5)

blocks.note: A + ROW, a row being a quarrel

annotation.surface: A dispute over which way a right-turn signal points.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Right indicator' suggests a car's turn signal; 'right' is just R and 'indicator' alone defines. Row, rhyming with cow, is British for a quarrel.
annotation.definitionFit: An arrow is a sign that indicates direction.

entries.clue: DIs go in to arrest second nonconformist (9)

indicatorNotes.to arrest: the DIs hold the second inside them

blocks.note: s = second, the unit of time
to enter is to go in

annotation.surface: Police detectives going in to arrest a second rebel.
annotation.walkthrough: The police raid is a false scene: 'DIs' are letters for a container, and 'second' is the time unit. A DI is a Detective Inspector in British police.
annotation.definitionFit: A dissenter refuses to conform to established opinion or church.

entries.clue: Run-down spot, extremely dodgy (5)

indicatorNotes.extremely: take the extremes, the first and last letters

annotation.surface: A shabby, very disreputable place.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Spot' reads as a noun, a place, but works as a verb. 'Extremely' looks like an intensifier for 'dodgy'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for a shabby, neglected place, from a plant gone to seed and past its best.
